```{r, include = FALSE}
has_suggests <- requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)
has_data <- has_suggests && nzchar(system.file("extdata", "diurnal_cycle.rds",
  package = "varunayan"
))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#",
  eval = has_data,
  fig.width = 10,
  fig.height = 6.5,
  fig.dpi = 150,
  warning = FALSE,
  message = FALSE,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

In this vignette, we compare the daily cycle of temperature, rainfall and
humidity in Mumbai (on the coast) and Bengaluru (on the Deccan plateau, 900 m).
We use `plot_radial_hourly()`, which draws hourly data as a 24-hour clock.
Midnight is at the top and the hours go clockwise. Each ring is a month, with
January at the centre, and each cell is the mean of that hour in that month.

```{r setup}
library(varunayan)
```

## Load the data

We downloaded hourly ERA5 for 2023 with `era5ify_point()`, at the CPCB stations
in Powai (Mumbai) and RVCE-Mailasandra (Bengaluru). For hourly data at one
point, `era5ify_point()` uses the CDS time-series endpoint.

```{r download, eval = FALSE}
mumbai <- era5ify_point(
  request_id = "diurnal_mumbai_2023",
  variables = c("2m_temperature", "2m_dewpoint_temperature", "total_precipitation"),
  start_date = "2023-01-01", end_date = "2023-12-31",
  lat = 19.1375, lon = 72.9151, frequency = "hourly"
)
```

The package includes the data for both cities.

```{r data}
hourly <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "diurnal_cycle.rds", package = "varunayan"))
head(hourly)
```

## Temperature

ERA5 times are in UTC, so we set `tz = "Asia/Kolkata"` to draw the hours in IST.

```{r temperature}
plot_radial_hourly(hourly, "temp_c",
  time = "time", by = "city", tz = "Asia/Kolkata",
  title = "2 m temperature, 2023", legend_title = "°C"
)
```

Both cities are warmest at 14:00. In Bengaluru, the day is 6 to 13 °C warmer
than the night in every month. In Mumbai, the difference is 9 to 15 °C in
winter and only 2 °C in July, when the monsoon clouds stop the daily cycle.

## Rainfall

ERA5 rainfall at each time is the total of the hour before it, so we set
`accumulated = TRUE`. In IST, each cell then covers half past one hour to half
past the next.

```{r rainfall}
plot_radial_hourly(hourly, "precip_mm",
  time = "time", by = "city", tz = "Asia/Kolkata", accumulated = TRUE, cmap = "Blues",
  title = "Mean hourly rainfall, 2023", legend_title = "mm per hour"
)
```

Mumbai gets rain from June to September, at all hours. Bengaluru gets rain in
more months, mostly in the late afternoon: 16:30 to 17:30 in the monsoon, an
hour earlier in October and November, and in the evening in April and May.

To show each day, we use `plot_radial()` with `agg = "sum"`.

```{r rain-calendar, fig.height = 6}
plot_radial(hourly, "precip_mm",
  time = "time", by = "city", agg = "sum", cmap = "Blues",
  title = "Daily rainfall, 2023", legend_title = "mm"
)
```

## Relative humidity

```{r humidity}
plot_radial_hourly(hourly, "rh",
  time = "time", by = "city", tz = "Asia/Kolkata", cmap = "YlGnBu",
  title = "Relative humidity, 2023", legend_title = "%"
)
```

Humidity is lowest at 14:00 in both cities. In January, it falls from 91 % at
05:00 to 35 % at 14:00 in Bengaluru. In July, Mumbai stays near 86 % all day.

Both functions take any column. Use `center = 0` for anomalies and
`rings = "day"` for one ring per day.
